data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The panel-plus-checklist's reliability gain is a manifestation of the wisdom-of-crowds effect: the checklist serves merely to anchor the panel on a common reference point, suppressing idiosyncratic variance; the expert, as a single individual, cannot average over their own internal noise.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the expert is allowed to make multiple judgments that are aggregated, the panel's advantage should diminish or vanish.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the panel members' judgments are correlated (e.g., they all attended the same training), the variance-reduction benefit is smaller than the model predicts.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the expert's intuition has low variance (high calibration), the panel's variance reduction offers no advantage.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the checklist introduces systematic bias, the variance reduction amplifies the bias rather than improving reliability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The expert's intuition is a single sample from a distribution of possible judgments the expert could have made. The panel, even without expertise, produces multiple samples. The checklist does not add information; it reduces variance by aligning the panel's judgments. The mean of multiple low-variance judgments is more reliable than a single high-variance judgment. The mechanism is statistical, not cognitive. The checklist is a variance-reduction tool, not an expertise-transfer device.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
